# Basic Principles of Statistical Inference

```{r}
#| label: setup-1
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
```

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After this chapter you should be able to:

1. Distinguish a **parameter** from a **statistic**.
2. Describe the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ and of $\hat{p}$: its mean, its
   standard error and its shape.
3. Use the Central Limit Theorem to find probabilities about $\bar{x}$ and $\hat{p}$.
4. Explain what a 95% confidence interval means.
5. Write the null and alternative hypotheses for a research question, and tell
   a one-sided test from a two-sided test.
6. Find critical values and the critical region from the $z$ table (Table 4).
7. Explain Type I and Type II errors in an economic setting.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Does This Matter?

Economists rarely see a whole population. The Ministry of Labour cannot ask
every worker in Chiang Mai about their wage, and the Bank of Thailand cannot
survey every household about its debt. Instead we take a **sample** and use it
to say something about the **population**.

Two samples from the same population give different answers. Statistical
inference tells us how much a sample result can vary, and so how far we can
trust it. This chapter builds the ideas used in every later chapter.
:::

## Parameters, Statistics and Sampling Distributions

A **parameter** describes a population. It is a fixed number, but usually unknown.
A **statistic** describes a sample. We can calculate it, but it changes from
sample to sample.

| | Population (parameter) | Sample (statistic) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{x}$ |
| Standard deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ |
| Variance | $\sigma^2$ | $s^2$ |
| Proportion | $p$ | $\hat{p}$ |
| Size | $N$ | $n$ |

The **sampling distribution** of a statistic is the distribution of its values
over all possible samples of the same size $n$.

```{r}
#| label: income-population
set.seed(272)
income_pop <- rlnorm(100000, meanlog = log(22000), sdlog = 0.65)
mu_inc <- mean(income_pop)
sd_inc <- sd(income_pop)

sim_means <- function(n, reps = 5000) {
  replicate(reps, mean(sample(income_pop, n)))
}
samp <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = "Population", value = income_pop),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 5", value = sim_means(5)),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 30", value = sim_means(30)),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 100", value = sim_means(100))
)
samp$panel <- factor(samp$panel, levels = c("Population", "Means, n = 5",
                                            "Means, n = 30", "Means, n = 100"))
```

**Example.** @fig-income-sampling uses a hypothetical population of
100,000 households. Monthly household income is skewed to the right: most
households earn a moderate amount and a few earn a great deal. The population
mean is $\mu$ = `r format(round(mu_inc), big.mark = ",")` baht and the
standard deviation is $\sigma$ = `r format(round(sd_inc), big.mark = ",")` baht.
The other panels show the means of 5,000 random samples of size 5, 30 and 100.

```{r}
#| label: fig-income-sampling
#| fig-cap: "Household income in a hypothetical population (top left) and the sampling distribution of the sample mean for n = 5, 30 and 100"
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(samp, aes(value / 1000)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_inc / 1000, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Monthly income (thousand baht)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Three things happen as $n$ grows:

1. The sample means are centred on the population mean $\mu$ (dashed line).
2. The spread of the sample means gets **smaller**.
3. The shape gets closer to a **normal** curve, even though the population is skewed.

## Standard Error and the Central Limit Theorem

The standard deviation of a sampling distribution is called the
**standard error (SE)**. It measures how much a statistic varies from sample to sample.

### Sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$

- Mean: $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$
- Standard error: $\displaystyle \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$
- Shape:
  - if the population is normal, $\bar{x}$ is normal for any $n$;
  - if not, $\bar{x}$ is **approximately normal** when $n$ is large ($n \ge 30$).
    This is the **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**.

So we can standardize $\bar{x}$ and use the $z$ table:
$$
z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}
$$

### Sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$

The sample proportion $\hat{p} = x/n$, where $x$ is the number of "successes".

- Mean: $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$
- Standard error: $\displaystyle \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$
- Shape: approximately normal when $np \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) \ge 5$.

$$
z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}
$$

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Larger samples, smaller error

Because $\sqrt{n}$ is in the denominator, a sample four times as large
halves the standard error.
:::

```{r}
#| label: ex-wage
w_mu <- 380; w_sigma <- 60; w_n <- 36
w_se <- w_sigma / sqrt(w_n)
w_z  <- (400 - w_mu) / w_se
w_F  <- round(pnorm(w_z), 4)

d_p <- 0.65; d_n <- 400
d_se <- round(sqrt(d_p * (1 - d_p) / d_n), 4)
d_z  <- round((0.60 - d_p) / d_se, 2)
d_F  <- round(pnorm(abs(d_z)), 4)
```

### Worked Example 1.1: daily wage

Suppose the daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai has mean
$\mu$ = `r w_mu` baht and standard deviation $\sigma$ = `r w_sigma` baht
(hypothetical figures). A random sample of $n$ = `r w_n` workers is taken.

(a) Describe the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$.
(b) Find the probability that the sample mean wage is more than 400 baht.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

(a) Since $n$ = `r w_n` $\ge 30$, by the CLT $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal with
$$
\mu_{\bar{x}} = `r w_mu`, \qquad
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{`r w_sigma`}{\sqrt{`r w_n`}} = `r w_se` \text{ baht.}
$$

(b)
$$
z = \frac{400 - `r w_mu`}{`r w_se`} = `r fmt(w_z, 2)`
$$
From Table 4, $P(Z \le `r fmt(w_z, 2)`) = `r fmt(w_F, 4)`$, so
$$
P(\bar{x} > 400) = P(Z > `r fmt(w_z, 2)`) = 1 - `r fmt(w_F, 4)` = `r fmt(1 - w_F, 4)`.
$$

About `r round(100 * (1 - w_F), 1)`% of samples of `r w_n` workers would have a mean
wage above 400 baht.
:::

### Worked Example 1.2: household debt

Suppose `r 100 * d_p`% of households in a region have outstanding debt
(hypothetical figure). A survey samples $n$ = `r d_n` households.
Find the probability that less than 60% of the sampled households have debt.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

Check the conditions: $np = `r d_n * d_p` \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) = `r d_n * (1 - d_p)` \ge 5$,
so $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal.
$$
\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{`r d_p`(1-`r d_p`)}{`r d_n`}} = `r fmt(d_se, 4)`
$$
$$
z = \frac{0.60 - `r d_p`}{`r fmt(d_se, 4)`} = `r fmt(d_z, 2)`
$$
Table 4 gives only positive $z$. By symmetry,
$$
P(\hat{p} < 0.60) = P(Z < `r fmt(d_z, 2)`) = P(Z > `r fmt(abs(d_z), 2)`)
= 1 - `r fmt(d_F, 4)` = `r fmt(1 - d_F, 4)`.
$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-1-1
y_mu <- 4500; y_sigma <- 900; y_n <- 81
y_se <- y_sigma / sqrt(y_n)
y_z  <- (4320 - y_mu) / y_se
y_F  <- round(pnorm(abs(y_z)), 4)

v_p <- 0.40; v_n <- 600
v_se <- round(sqrt(v_p * (1 - v_p) / v_n), 4)
v_z  <- round((0.45 - v_p) / v_se, 2)
v_F  <- round(pnorm(v_z), 4)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 1.1

The monthly rent of rooms near a university has mean `r format(y_mu, big.mark = ",")`
baht and standard deviation `r y_sigma` baht (hypothetical figures). A random sample of
`r y_n` rooms is taken. Find

(a) the standard error of $\bar{x}$, and
(b) the probability that the sample mean rent is less than 4,320 baht.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="8"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 1.1"}
(a) $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = `r y_sigma` / \sqrt{`r y_n`} = `r y_se`$ baht.

(b) $z = (4320 - `r y_mu`) / `r y_se` = `r fmt(y_z, 2)`$, so
$P(\bar{x} < 4320) = P(Z > `r fmt(abs(y_z), 2)`) = 1 - `r fmt(y_F, 4)` = `r fmt(1 - y_F, 4)`$.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 1.2

In a province, `r 100 * v_p`% of workers are in the informal sector
(hypothetical figure). A labour force survey samples `r v_n` workers. Find the
probability that more than 45% of the sample work in the informal sector.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="8"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 1.2"}
$np = `r v_n * v_p`$ and $n(1-p) = `r v_n * (1 - v_p)`$ are both at least 5.
$\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{`r v_p`(`r 1 - v_p`)/`r v_n`} = `r fmt(v_se, 4)`$,
$z = (0.45 - `r v_p`)/`r fmt(v_se, 4)` = `r fmt(v_z, 2)`$, so
$P(\hat{p} > 0.45) = 1 - `r fmt(v_F, 4)` = `r fmt(1 - v_F, 4)`$.
:::

## The Idea of a Confidence Interval

A single number such as $\bar{x}$ is a **point estimate**. It is almost never
exactly equal to $\mu$. A **confidence interval (CI)** gives a range of
plausible values instead:
$$
\text{point estimate} \;\pm\; (\text{critical value}) \times \text{SE}
$$

The **confidence level** (for example 95%) describes the method, not one
interval: if we took many samples and built a 95% CI from each, about 95% of
the intervals would contain the true parameter.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ci-sim
#| fig-cap: "Forty 95% confidence intervals for the mean daily wage, each from a different sample of 36 workers (hypothetical population with mean 380 baht). Red intervals miss the true mean."
#| fig-height: 4.5
set.seed(2721)
z975 <- crit_z(0.975)
cis <- data.frame(sample = 1:40,
                  xbar = replicate(40, mean(rnorm(w_n, w_mu, w_sigma))))
cis$lower <- cis$xbar - z975 * w_se
cis$upper <- cis$xbar + z975 * w_se
cis$covers <- cis$lower <= w_mu & cis$upper >= w_mu
n_miss <- sum(!cis$covers)
ggplot(cis, aes(y = sample, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, colour = covers)) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar), size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = w_mu, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Daily wage (baht)", y = "Sample")
```

In @fig-ci-sim, `r 40 - n_miss` of the 40 intervals contain $\mu$ = `r w_mu` and
`r n_miss` do not. For a single interval we write:

> We are 95% confident that the mean daily wage is between ... and ... baht.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## A common mistake

Do not say "there is a 95% probability that $\mu$ is in this interval".
Once the interval is calculated, $\mu$ is either in it or not. The 95% refers
to how often the method works.
:::

Chapters 2 and 3 give the formula of the CI for each parameter.

## The Logic of Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test uses sample data to decide between two statements about a
population parameter.

- The **null hypothesis** $H_0$ is the statement of "no change" or "no
  difference". It always contains the equals sign.
- The **alternative hypothesis** $H_1$ is what the researcher wants to show.
  It contains $\ne$, $<$ or $>$.

We assume $H_0$ is true and ask whether the sample result is unusual under that
assumption. If it is, we reject $H_0$.

**Example.** The Ministry of Labour reports that the mean daily wage of
construction workers is 380 baht. A labour union believes the mean is lower.
$$
H_0: \mu = 380 \qquad H_1: \mu < 380
$$

The direction in $H_1$ comes from the **research question**, never from the data.

| Research question | $H_1$ | Test | Critical region |
|:---|:---:|:---|:---|
| Is it different from $\mu_0$? | $\mu \ne \mu_0$ | two-sided | both tails, area $\alpha/2$ each |
| Is it less than $\mu_0$? | $\mu < \mu_0$ | one-sided (left) | left tail, area $\alpha$ |
| Is it greater than $\mu_0$? | $\mu > \mu_0$ | one-sided (right) | right tail, area $\alpha$ |

### Test statistic, critical value and critical region

- The **test statistic** measures how far the sample result is from $H_0$, in
  standard errors. For example $z_{\text{cal}} = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$.
- The **level of significance** $\alpha$ is the probability of rejecting $H_0$
  when $H_0$ is true. We usually use $\alpha$ = 0.05.
- The **critical value** separates the values of the test statistic that lead
  to rejecting $H_0$ from those that do not.
- The **critical region** is the set of values that lead to rejecting $H_0$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-regions
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-cap: "Critical regions for a z test at alpha = 0.05"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Two-sided"
#|   - "Left-sided"
#|   - "Right-sided"
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-width: 3.3
crit_plot("z", "two")
crit_plot("z", "left")
crit_plot("z", "right")
```

**Decision rule.** If $z_{\text{cal}}$ falls in the critical region, we reject
$H_0$. Otherwise we accept $H_0$.

### Writing the hypotheses

**Worked Example 1.3.** Write $H_0$ and $H_1$.

(a) A price-monitoring agency checks whether the mean price of a 5-kg bag of
rice has changed from 210 baht.
(b) An economist claims that more than 30% of households in Chiang Mai have
used a government stimulus measure.
(c) A bank claims that the mean monthly loan payment of its customers is less
than 8,000 baht.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

(a) $H_0: \mu = 210 \quad H_1: \mu \ne 210$ (two-sided: "changed" has no direction)
(b) $H_0: p = 0.30 \quad H_1: p > 0.30$ (right-sided)
(c) $H_0: \mu = 8000 \quad H_1: \mu < 8000$ (left-sided)
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 1.3

Write $H_0$ and $H_1$, and say whether each test is two-sided, left-sided or right-sided.

(a) A researcher tests whether the mean household debt in a district is higher
than 200,000 baht.
(b) An analyst tests whether the proportion of firms that raised prices last
quarter is different from 0.50.
(c) A manager tests whether a new pricing strategy has reduced the mean number
of days a product stays in stock below 14 days.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="6"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 1.3"}
(a) $H_0: \mu = 200000 \quad H_1: \mu > 200000$ (right-sided)
(b) $H_0: p = 0.50 \quad H_1: p \ne 0.50$ (two-sided)
(c) $H_0: \mu = 14 \quad H_1: \mu < 14$ (left-sided)
:::

## Type I and Type II Errors

The decision is based on a sample, so it can be wrong.

| | $H_0$ is true | $H_0$ is false |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| **Reject $H_0$** | Type I error (probability $\alpha$) | Correct decision |
| **Accept $H_0$** | Correct decision | Type II error (probability $\beta$) |

**Example.** The government tests whether a stimulus measure increased mean
household spending.
$H_0$: the measure had no effect; $H_1$: the measure increased spending.

- **Type I error:** concluding that the measure worked when it did not. The
  government may continue an expensive policy that has no effect.
- **Type II error:** concluding that the measure did not work when it did. The
  government may stop a useful policy.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Choosing $\alpha$

A smaller $\alpha$ makes a Type I error less likely but a Type II error more
likely, for the same sample size. A larger sample reduces both.
:::

## Reading Statistical Tables

All the tables used in this course (Tables 4--7) give the **area to the left**
of a value. The subscript in our notation is that area:
$z_{0.975}$ is the value with area 0.975 to its left.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Two steps for every critical value

1. Draw the curve and **shade the area to the left** of the value you need.
2. Read the table at that left-tail area.
:::

The $z$ table (Table 4) gives $P(Z \le z)$ for $z$ from 0.00 to 3.49. The
bottom row also lists the most common values:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-z-bottom
#| tbl-cap: "Common critical values of z (bottom row of Table 4)"
zp <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.975, 0.99, 0.995)
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Area to the left` = fmt(zp, 3),
                        z = fmt(sapply(zp, crit_z), 3), check.names = FALSE),
             align = "cc")
```

Table 4 has only positive $z$. Because the normal curve is symmetric,
$z_{0.05} = -z_{0.95}$ and $z_{0.025} = -z_{0.975}$.

**Worked Example 1.4.** Find the critical value(s) and critical region for a
$z$ test with $\alpha$ = 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

| $H_1$ | Area to the left | Critical value(s) | Critical region |
|:---:|:---|:---:|:---|
| $\ne$ | 0.025 and 0.975 | $z_{0.025} = `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$, $z_{0.975} = `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`$ |
| $<$ | 0.05 | $z_{0.05} = `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$ |
| $>$ | 0.95 | $z_{0.95} = `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$ | $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$ |
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 1.4

For each test, shade the area to the left on the curve first, then find the
critical value(s) and write the critical region.

(a) $H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.01
(b) $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.01
(c) $H_1: p < p_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.10
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-yt-1-4
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-cap: "Shade the area to the left before reading Table 4"
#| fig-subcap: ["", "", ""]
#| fig-height: 1.8
#| fig-width: 3.2
blank_curve("z"); blank_curve("z"); blank_curve("z")
```

::: {.workspace lines="6"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 1.4"}
(a) Areas 0.005 and 0.995: $z_{0.995} = `r fmt(crit_z(.995), 3)`$.
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.995), 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.995), 3)`$.

(b) Area 0.99: $z_{0.99} = `r fmt(crit_z(.99), 3)`$. Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.99), 3)`$.

(c) Area 0.10: $z_{0.10} = -z_{0.90} = `r fmt(-crit_z(.90), 3)`$.
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.90), 3)`$.
:::

## Formula Summary {.unnumbered}

| Statistic | Mean | Standard error | Normal when | $z$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|:---:|
| $\bar{x}$ | $\mu$ | $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ | population normal, or $n \ge 30$ | $\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ |
| $\hat{p}$ | $p$ | $\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}$ | $np \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) \ge 5$ | $\dfrac{\hat{p}-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}$ |

| $H_1$ | Critical region ($z$ test) |
|:---:|:---|
| $\ne$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}$ |
| $<$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}$ |
| $>$ | $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}$ |

```{r}
#| label: exercises-1
e1_mu <- 45; e1_sigma <- 4; e1_n <- 64
e1_se <- e1_sigma / sqrt(e1_n)
e1_z1 <- (44.2 - e1_mu) / e1_se; e1_F1 <- round(pnorm(abs(e1_z1)), 4)
e1_z2 <- (46 - e1_mu) / e1_se;   e1_F2 <- round(pnorm(e1_z2), 4)
e5_p <- 0.05
```

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

**1.1** The price of a kilogram of pork at fresh markets has mean `r e1_mu`
baht and standard deviation `r e1_sigma` baht (hypothetical figures). A random sample of `r e1_n` markets is taken.

(a) Find the standard error of $\bar{x}$.
(b) Find $P(\bar{x} < 44.2)$.
(c) Find $P(44.2 < \bar{x} < 46)$.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.1"}
(a) $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = `r e1_sigma`/\sqrt{`r e1_n`} = `r e1_se`$ baht.

(b) $z = (44.2 - `r e1_mu`)/`r e1_se` = `r fmt(e1_z1, 2)`$;
$P(\bar{x} < 44.2) = 1 - `r fmt(e1_F1, 4)` = `r fmt(1 - e1_F1, 4)`$.

(c) $z = (46 - `r e1_mu`)/`r e1_se` = `r fmt(e1_z2, 2)`$;
$P(44.2 < \bar{x} < 46) = `r fmt(e1_F2, 4)` - `r fmt(1 - e1_F1, 4)` = `r fmt(e1_F2 - (1 - e1_F1), 4)`$.
:::

**1.2** Write $H_0$ and $H_1$.

(a) The Bank of Thailand tests whether mean headline inflation over the past
year was above its 3% upper target.
(b) A researcher tests whether the proportion of graduates who find a job within
six months differs from 0.70.
(c) A firm tests whether a discount campaign reduced the mean time to sell a
product below 20 days.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.2"}
(a) $H_0: \mu = 3 \quad H_1: \mu > 3$
(b) $H_0: p = 0.70 \quad H_1: p \ne 0.70$
(c) $H_0: \mu = 20 \quad H_1: \mu < 20$
:::

**1.3** Find the critical value(s) and the critical region of a $z$ test.

(a) $H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.10
(b) $H_1: \mu < \mu_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.01
(c) $H_1: p > p_0$, $\alpha$ = 0.05

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.3"}
(a) $z_{0.95} = `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$: reject $H_0$ if $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$.
(b) $z_{0.01} = -z_{0.99} = `r fmt(-crit_z(.99), 3)`$: reject $H_0$ if $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.99), 3)`$.
(c) $z_{0.95} = `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$: reject $H_0$ if $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$.
:::

**1.4** A provincial office tests whether a job-training programme raised the
mean monthly income of participants. $H_0$: the programme has no effect on mean
income; $H_1$: the programme raises mean income. Describe a Type I error and a
Type II error in this context, and give one consequence of each.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.4"}
Type I error: concluding that the programme raises income when it does not.
Budget may continue to be spent on a programme that does not work.
Type II error: concluding that the programme has no effect when it does raise
income. A useful programme may be cut.
:::

**1.5** The unemployment rate in a province is `r 100 * e5_p`% (hypothetical
figure). Can the normal approximation be used for $\hat{p}$ when (a) $n$ = 80,
(b) $n$ = 200? Explain.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.5"}
(a) $np = 80(`r e5_p`) = `r 80 * e5_p` < 5$, so the normal approximation should not be used.
(b) $np = 200(`r e5_p`) = `r 200 * e5_p`$ and $n(1-p) = `r 200 * (1 - e5_p)`$ are both at
least 5, so it can be used.
:::

**1.6** A 95% CI for the mean monthly electricity bill of households in a city
is 1,120 to 1,280 baht. Which statements are correct?

(a) We are 95% confident that the mean monthly electricity bill of all
households in the city is between 1,120 and 1,280 baht.
(b) 95% of households in the city pay between 1,120 and 1,280 baht per month.
(c) If we took many samples and built a 95% CI from each, about 95% of the
intervals would contain the population mean.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 1.6"}
(a) and (c) are correct. (b) is wrong: the interval is about the population
mean, not about individual households.
:::
